title: The buffer pool: pin, dirty, LRU, and CLOCK
lead: Track one shared page, then trace every replacement in a three-frame buffer pool.
goals: Update pin counts and dirty flags correctly
Simulate LRU and CLOCK when some pages are pinned
Explain sequential flooding and the limits of replacement policies

sections.title: Keep a page in RAM while someone is using it
sections.html:
Two operations need records on the same disk page P. Reading P twice would waste work if the first copy is still in RAM. The DBMS keeps a pool of memory spaces called frames, each holding one page. This is the buffer pool. Its page table answers “which frame currently holds P?”

If F0 already contains P, a request is a hit: use F0 without reading disk. If P is absent, it is a miss: choose a free frame or replace a page, then read P. A page ID identifies stored data; a frame ID identifies a reusable RAM location. The same frame can later hold another page.

Suppose operation A receives P's address in F0. If B replaces F0 with Q before A finishes, A will use the wrong bytes. A pin count records active uses: pin(P) increments it; a matching unpin(P,modified) decrements it. Only pin=0 frames are candidates for replacement. Releasing P need not evict it immediately; keeping it can serve a later hit.

  1. On a hit, find the resident frame and increment its pin count.
  2. On a miss, obtain a free frame or an unpinned victim.
  3. If the victim is dirty, preserve its changed contents before overwriting it under the required persistence protocol.
  4. Read the requested page, mark the incoming copy clean, set pin=1, and return its address.
  5. After use, unpin and report whether this use modified the page.

Dirty means modified in RAM since the stored copy was written. Pin answers whether someone still uses the frame; dirty answers whether RAM has unpersisted changes. These mechanisms do not replace transaction concurrency control or crash recovery.

Try: every frame has pin>0. Can LRU choose the oldest anyway?

No. Eligibility comes before policy ranking. The implementation must wait, report lack of a frame or use another management mechanism; it cannot overwrite an actively used frame.

Is pinning a replacement for transaction concurrency control?

No. It protects frame use, while concurrency control coordinates conflicting data operations.

sections.title: A release can leave a dirty page behind
sections.html:
Track one resident page P rather than treating release as save. Two users access it:

EventPin afterwardDirty afterwardReason
Initial0falseNo active use or unpersisted change
A: pin(P)1falseOne active use
B: pin(P)2falseTwo active uses
A modifies; unpin(P,true)1trueOne user remains; preserve modification
B reads; unpin(P,false)0trueB made no new change; A’s change remains

The dirty update is old_dirty OR modified_by_this_use. TRUE OR FALSE stays TRUE. B's false argument does not declare the whole page clean. Pin=0 makes P eligible for replacement, but it can remain cached.

If absent Q arrives and P is chosen, this simplified transfer count adds one write to preserve P and one read to load Q. Q then has pin=1 and dirty=false. Count the write separately from the miss. Preserving P must obey recovery requirements such as log-before-data, developed in Lecture 21; arbitrary write order is not implied.

Forgetting an unpin can leave a frame permanently ineligible after its user finishes. Clearing an earlier dirty flag can lose a modification when discarding the page. Correct pin bookkeeping also does not prevent conflicting logical writes; that needs separate coordination.

Try: C pins P immediately after both users release. Does C need a disk read?

If P remained resident, C hits and pin becomes 1; dirty stays true. No read is needed, and P cannot be evicted until C releases it.

Key takeaway

Pin count and the dirty flag answer different questions. Pin=0 means nobody still holds the page; dirty=true means there are changes not yet written to disk. Unpinning with false says only that this user made no modification. It does not erase an earlier user’s dirty state.

After the second unpin(false), is P clean?

No. Pin count becomes zero but the earlier modification leaves dirty=true.

Current explanation scope: official PDF physical pages 9–11. Numerical fixtures are original teaching examples.

sections.title: Write every state of a three-frame LRU run
sections.html:
Several unpinned pages compete for space. LRU, least recently used, replaces the eligible page whose last use is furthest in the past. The lecture timestamps the most recent unpin, the end of use. In this original trace each request pins then immediately unpins, so last-access and last-unpin orders agree.

Three frames start empty; every page is clean. Requests are A,B,C,A,D,B,A,C. The order below is oldest → newest use, not physical frame order:

RequestHit/missVictimResident order afterwardMisses so far
AMissNoneA1
BMissNoneA,B2
CMissNoneA,B,C3
AHitNoneB,C,A3
DMissBC,A,D4
BMissCA,D,B5
AHitNoneD,B,A5
CMissDB,A,C6

The first A hit needs no read but makes A most recent. Thus D replaces B, although A was loaded first. FIFO instead ranks load time; a hit does not refresh its insertion order.

Total: six misses, two hits, zero write-backs. The first three misses fill free frames; later misses replace B,C,D. If D is dirty when evicted, misses remain six and one write is added. Misses count absent requested pages; writes count dirty victims that must be preserved.

Run the trace in the buffer lab with A→1,B→2,C→3,D→4: enter 1,2,3,1,4,2,1,3, three frames and LRU. The lab assumes clean, unpinned pages and does not simulate pinning or CLOCK. By contrast, repeating A,B,C,D with three LRU frames misses every time: the fourth page evicts the page needed next, repeatedly. This is sequential flooding; recent use need not predict future use.

Try: repeat A,B,C,D with four frames instead. What changes?

The first four requests miss while filling the pool. Later requests hit if pages remain resident: the entire four-page working set now fits.

Key takeaway

Count cache misses and write-backs separately. A miss means the requested page is absent from the pool. In this model, an extra write occurs only when a dirty page must be replaced; six misses do not mean six writes.

If the evicted D is dirty, do the six misses become seven?

No. Misses remain six; add one write-back separately.

Current explanation scope: official PDF physical pages 13–14, 22–27. Numerical fixtures are original teaching examples.

sections.title: Give a page a second chance, then compare workloads
sections.html:
Exact recency bookkeeping costs work on each access. CLOCK keeps less history: a reference bit per frame and a hand moving around a ring. Increasing pin count sets ref=1 in the lecture's convention. At replacement, skip pinned frames; clear an unpinned ref=1 and continue; an unpinned ref=0 can be the victim.

Original state: hand at F0; F0 holds A(pin=1,ref=1), F1 holds B(pin=0,ref=1), F2 holds C(pin=0,ref=0). Load D:

Hand visitsActionChange
F0: ASkip: pinnedA stays protected
F1: BSecond chanceB.ref: 1→0
F2: CChoose victimReplace C with D
After loadHand advances to F0D: pin=1,ref=1

If C initially had ref=1, the first sweep clears B and C. With no intervening requests, the next sweep skips A and chooses B, now ref=0. CLOCK approximates recency; it does not ignore pin safety.

Can replacing the most recently used page help? With immediate unpin, clean pages and three empty frames, trace A,B,C,D,A,B,C,D using MRU. A,B,C miss; D misses and replaces C; A,B hit; C misses and replaces B; D hits. That is five misses. LRU misses all eight because its victim is needed next. MRU helps this scan pattern, while hot-page reuse can favour LRU.

LRU-K considers deeper reference history. Systems may partition budgets, use priority hints or prefetch. Incorrect prefetch consumes I/O and displaces useful pages. Every policy must still respect pin eligibility and persistence rules for dirty victims.

Try: leave C pinned when D arrives in the MRU trace. Can MRU evict it?

No. “Most recent” ranks eligible pages only. The five-miss result depended on immediate unpin; changing that assumption requires a new trace.

Can the MRU example evict C if C remains pinned?

No. Policy ranking only applies to eligible victims; a pinned frame is ineligible.

quiz.question: P has dirty=true. What is dirty after unpin(P,false)?
options: It depends on the pin count
quiz.explanation: The new dirty flag is the old dirty flag OR the supplied dirty argument. true OR false remains true.
